speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRUST COMPANIES A.CT LENDING AND INVESTMENT POWERS
speechtext:
Section 1 of this bill is designed to correct an obvious misprint in the present revised statutes, subsections (3) and (4) of section 3 of chapter 29. Section 2 of the bill is intended to make uniform the lending and investment [DOT] powers of all trust companies, regardless of the date of incorporation. The Trust Companies Act was first passed in 1914, and applied as a whole to companies incorporated after the date it came into force. It had only a limited application to companies incorporated earlier, the limitation being set forth in subsections (3) and (4) of section 3, in which two groups of sections, 62 to 88 and 83 to 90 are stated to apply to companies incorporated before 1914. These two groups overlap so that it is impossible to say what is intended as respects section 81. It seems probable that 88 is a misprint for 80. and that section 81 is not made applicable to those companies.
The amendment in section 1 o-f the bill will make it clear that section 81 applies bo all companies.
Section 2 of the bill will make uniform for the future the lending and investment powers of all companies. The reference to the Corn-

Maple Products

panics Act in the section, inserted by section 2 of the bill, is made necessary for the following reasons:
The special acts incorporating the older trust companies contain a provision making the former Companies Clauses Act, or part II of the Companies Act, revised statutes, 1906, chapter 79, applicable to the company incorporated and in the said act or part there was one section (revised statutes, 1906, chapter 79, section 167) declaring that the company should not lend any of its funds to any shareholder. This restriction still applies and is found in section 189 of the present Companies Act, 1934, chapter 33.
By amendments to the Trust Companies Act in 1922 (chapter 51, section 8) and 1924 (chapter 71, section 4) it was provided that all such restrictions on investment powers should be repealed, but unfortunately those sections were not carried into the groups of sections in section 3 of the act declared to apply to the older companies.
The Companies Act, section 146, still provides that the restriction in section 189 shall continue to apply to the older companies unless "expressly varied or excepted by the special act".
There has been an amendment proposed in the other house, in which the word "to" is changed to "by". That is the only change.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRISONERS OF WAR AND INTERNEES-PORT ARTHUR DISTRICT
speechtext:
1.	There are 2,572 German prisoners of war employed in lumber camps in the Port Arthur district, and no Japanese internees.
2.	The employer pays to the crown $2.50 per working day for the services of each prisoner of war, from which an amount of 50c per working day is credited to the account of the prisoner of war.
3.	As of November 30, 1945, there were 727 males registered for employment. Of these 269 have been referred to jobs but the results are not yet known. It should be mentioned that these people are not necessarily unemployed. They may be changing from one job to another.
All of the males who have registered for employment in Port Arthur and Fort William have been given an opportunity to take a job in lumber camps and those that have accepted the offer have been sent to the camps.

speechtext:
On Saturday of last week the hon. member for Vancouver East asked if I had received representations from certain student bodies, graduates of universities, col-

Bretton Woods Agreements
leges and the like, in favour of a reduction of fares on railways during the holiday season. I have personally received no such representations other than those from my hon. friend and from the hon. member for Vancouver South, and a resolution which the hon. member for Vancouver East sent me this morning.
I have canvassed the situation carefully, and I find that conditions with reference to the railways are such that it would be impossible to grant the request. In fact, the equipment, services and man-powrer of the railways to-day are taxed to such a capacity that it would, I think, at this season be a mistake to consent to the request. I am this day making a press release on the whole situation and I would like to call the attention of the house to one or two features of it. It points to the fact that the Queen Elizabeth is arriving at New York on December 27, having on board some 13,000 troops, and that will require movement from the port of New York to various parts of Canada of. about twenty-five full trains, including sleeping cars, diners, baggage cars and day coaches. Arrivals at Halifax include the Puncher on December 21, with 800 service men; the Lady Rodney on December 25, with 500; the Duchess of Bedford on December 29, with 3,000, and the Mauritania on January 3, with 6,000. It will take, to transport these troops from Halifax to various parts of Canada, every bit of available equipment. The army, air force and navy authorities are granting five days' leave at Christmas and New Years to fifty per cent of the armed forces, and that, together with the very heavy volume of freight traffic then moving in all directions and to -the seaports particularly, makes the position a very serious one.
While I sympathize keenly with those who have made this request, the university and college students, I am sure that hon. members and the house will agree that under the circumstances priority must of necessity be given the armed forces.

The house resumed from Saturday, December 8, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
That it is expedient to present a measure to grant authority to accept on behalf of Canada and to carry out the obligations of Canada under the articles of agreement for an international monetary fund and an international hank for reconstruction and development prepared by the united nations monetary and financial conference held at Bretton Woods in July, 1944; to authorize the payment of the subscriptions required from Canada out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund to an amount not exceeding seven hundred million dollars; and to authorize the borrowing under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, of sums not exceeding seven hundred million dollars.

speechtext:
The stand which our group is taking is based in part oni the assumption that there is no real reason for rushing this measure through. There is no real reason for using any kind of high pressure methods in order to secure the passing of the Bretton Woods agreement. I am not implying that this has been done, but w'e do not
Bretton Woods Agreements

think that there is any urgency about the matter. In fact, we are inclined to believe that a royal commission should be appointed to consider the whole question of the Bretton Woods agreement. We have just had sitting in Canada a royal commission studying the question of the taxing of cooperatives. That commission has been at work for months. It has had the power to call witnesses and examine them. The taxation of cooperatives is so insignificant, in contrast with the question of the Bretton Woods agreement, as to be almost, contemptible comparatively. Yet we are supposed to be crowding this thing through. We have had royal commissions on various topics and they have sat for many months, though they have not been nearly as important as the question we are considering, nor has the truth been so difficult to arrive at. We believe that we are working in the best interests of the government in this matter.
In days to come this country, if it rushes precipitately into the acceptance of the Bretton Woods proposals, could be accused of helping to bring pressure to bear upon Britain in making her decision on the agreement. I do not wish to emphasize too strongly what I am about to say, but I am almost afraid that lurking in the minds of hon. members is the belief that for some reason or other Canada is bound to go through with this undertaking, that something terrible will happen if she does not accept the Bretton Woods proposals, that there is perhaps a threat of some kind on the part of some person or persons. I do not know. If the government is behaving as it is behaving because of external pressure brought to bear either by nations outside or by people within those nations it is an exceedingly serious* matter, and all I can say is that Canada ought to know. If we are to be hanged by someone, we ought to know who that someone is and why he intends to hang us, and we certainly should not be expected to go up docilely and put the noose round our own necks and draw it tight.
Canada is in the best possible position to oppose Bretton Woods. Except for the United States, of all nations that are being, I am afraid, high-pressured into the acceptance of the proposals Canada is the most nearly selfsufficient, Canada is therefore more able t-o offer successful resistance to any sort of attack, or any attempt to force her, than any other country. She is im an immeasurably better position than Britain, and consequently we should have courage enough to take a stand.
fMr. Blackmore.]
Furthermore, she is the eldest of the sisters in the commonwealth. What she does will have a special significance all over the world and particularly in Britain.
I suggest therefore that the government should act with the greatest discretion and moderation in considering this measure. I would even suggest that it would be well advised even now to withdraw the Bretton Woods agreement and give the house time enough to study the whole matter, at any rate until the next session. But if the government has made up its mind that it does not intend to withdraw this resolution we must go on with the problem before us. I want it clearly understood that this group is not necessarily putting up any fight against Bretton Woods. That is not the object of our action at all. The impression is being created in the country that the Social Credit group in the House of Commons is engaging in a filibuster, but that simply is not true.

speechtext:
That is so, and I
recognize the hon. gentleman's very sincere interest. However, I want to make clear the position of the Social Crediters.
Public servants can be guilty of culpable ignorance, culpable negligence and culpable cowardice. In regard to the Bretton Woods agreement it is dangerously easy to be all three. At the present time as far as members of parliament are concerned it is dangerously [DOT]difficult not to be culpably ignorant, culpably negligent and culpably cowardly in respect to the Brettton Woods agreement. I have read through the Final Act a dozen times at least. It is long; it is dry; it is technical and abstruse. It deals with matters unfamiliar to all but those with the most highly specialized knowledge and training. It bears evidence of having been drafted by a past master of the art of tricky phrasing to confuse, the mind, becloud the real issues and conceal the real purport behind the document. Paul Einzig points this out very definitely in a statement which I think we have put on record already and to which hon. members can refer. He says the return to gold has been covered up in this document, and goes on to talk about the almost incomprehensible jargon that is used.
Continuing to deal with the diffculties an hon. member faces in regard to this matter; the resolution was introduced on December 6, only nine days before the date agreed upon for the
closing of parliament and only fifteen sitting days before Christmas. Let us just recall the. number of days an ordinary royal commission spends considering the taxation of cooperatives, for example, and contrast that with the position of this house or the position of the banking and commerce committee, if the resolution gets to it. The resolution was introduced in the closing -weeks of a three months' session of a new parliament, including a very large percentage of new men attending their first session of parliament and consequently naturally unable to catch very much of an impression as to what it is all about, if they are anything like I was when I first came here. The Bretton Woods matter appears on a crowded and heavy agenda on which were such weighty matters as the Aeronautics Act; the housing and central mortgage act; the citizenship measure; the flag resolution; bill 15; the war appropriation bill and the united nations charter, a matter which alone should have occupied the house steadily for at least one month. I have not previously expressed my definite opinon with regard to the united nations charter and the way this house dealt with it, but I am going to say now that the way we dealt with the united nations charter was a positive reflection on this house and on parliamentary government the whole world over. Each of these considerations was a difficult matter, involving fundamental issues and unpredictable implications. Most of them required intensive reading and rigid concentration. And while the house was grinding its way through this repelling programme each member was literally beset with letters raising various problems requiring most careful attention and effort. How could the average member find enough energy and the opportunity to sufficiently study the problem of Bretton, Woods?
Then we come to the next aspect of it. It is unpopular to oppose Bretton Woods. Every hon. member who has been in this house for any length of time knows how difficult it is to keep one's foot on the ground and maintain a cool head when he begins to get letters, begins to read editorials, begins to read attacks reflecting upon his stand in the house and telling him. what he should do. I repeat, it is unpopular to oppose Bretton Woods. Propaganda agencies have laboured assiduously for five years conditioning public opinion. The hon. member for Peace River referred to this in his speech the [DOT] other day. Starting with "union now" and "federal union" and a whole library of books and periodicals they began to build up public opinion for this very measure. People have been lashed into almost a frenzy
Bretton Woods Agreements

about war and peace; they have been stampeded into the obsession that only the surrender of sovereignty would guarantee peace. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin pointed out the other night a number of cases in which obviously an attempt was being made to stampede public opinion. The people have been thrown into such a state of panic over their disease that they were prepared to swallow any suggested medicine without even examining the label or the directions on the outside of the bottle. In this day of free debate, this day of the radio and large scale methods of conveying information, this is astonishing; it is amazing that a people could be so much affected. But there it is. Anyone who calls for even a sense of caution is likely to be accused of committing some sort of sacrilege. This was quite obvious in the united nations discussions. One was not supposed even to talk about it. One mentioned it with bated breath, as he would the name of the divinity.
That sort of thing is not conducive to sane, reasoned behaviour. We find it in this instance. Members of parliament are faced with every temptation to neglect their duty in respect of Bretton Woods. Naturally they desire to get through and to go home. I want to get through and to go home too. I have just as lovely and pleasant a fireside to go back to as has any other hon. member. I want to be there. But I can remember when my boys were in the army-as one of them still is. They could not go home when duty called. And I might saj', incidentally, that my boy who died did not do it for such a base betrayal as Bretton Woods. My boy died for the British empire, that it might be great and free. And this wretched Bretton Woods thing has been foisted upon us-almost before he was buried.
These are matters of serious import. The government's whole attitude, as we gather from the minister's excellent speech, is based upon a fallacy. This may come as a shock to some people, but it is one of the best evidences that this house should proceed writh the greatest possible caution.
May I refer to a passage in the minister's speech-and I am sure he will follow me, and will correct me if I draw any false conclusions. I ask hon. members to tell me if I draw any false conclusions. At page 3089 of Hansard we find this:
When the great depression struck, each country had to cope as best it could with the situation. The minister is a most honest man, and I know he wants to .have everything exactly straight. So am I an honest man-at least I like to think I am. I can learn from the minister, and perhaps between us we can improve our standards of understanding.
What was the cause of the depression? Well, the first important cause was the cessation of United States foreign lending. At the moment that the foreign lending, which during the roaring twenties had been so extensive, began to diminish, and the foreign lenders began to worry about their lending, they began to withdraw. Immediately many of the great business concerns in. the United States which had been, assured of markets abroad now saw where their markets were to be restricted. The result was that they began immediately to restrict their operations, and the banking system began to retrench. That was^ the first step toward the depression.
The second step is one about which there has been some discussion, and I am sure the minister will tell me whether he thinks I have been correctly informed or otherwise. Of course we must depend upon the works we read. The information I get is that the second step in the depression was the raising of the rediscount rate by the federal reserve board in the United States. Certainly that took place. AVhat effect did it have? Well, the very moment that the rediscount rate was raised by the federal reserve board, the banks automatical!}' began to recall their loans and to restrict their credit. This began to precipitate the deflation which resulted in falling prices, and all the other ills which came naturally with the depression.
The' third cause of the depression was a loss of confidence in securities by speculators. Hon. members will recall that in 1928 and 1929 the first sign of illness was the flutter on the Wall street stock market.

speechtext: I appreciate your intervention. I wish to restate that I have no desire at all to say anything that is not entirely true.' Naturally it was the two causes which I have already given. First, there was a cessation of foreign lending on the part of prominent people in the United States and, second, there was the raising of the rediscount rate by the federal reserve board which made it much more difficult for banks to get money with which to lend money. The result was that those who were dealing in securities were unable to get credit; they became cautious and they tried to get rid of their 'holdings. The result was a general lack of confidence in the securities market which caused a catastrophic fall in prices generally. I am speaking from memory, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong, but as I recall what Irving Fisher said in his "One Hundred Per Cent Money," of the 823 billion of purchasing power which was out in circulation in the United States at the beginning of the trouble, $8 billion were withdrawn, leaving only $15 billion of purchasing power or money in circulation to do the work which $23 billion had done. May I commend the hon. member for Musk oka-Ontario for asking a question of that kind. It indicates an honest and sincere endeavour to work one's way through to an understanding of the whole situation, an understanding upon which an intelligent estimate of the whole Bretton Woods question can be developed.
The fourth step in the coming on of the depression was the calling of loans and the withdrawal of circulating mediums. As I have indicated, $8 billion of United States circulating mediums were withdrawn. Fifth, was the fall in prices which resulted in $200 billion of value in the United States being destroyed through the fall in prices of farms and all that sort of thing.
I would like to ask hon. members of the committee this simple question: If Bretton Woods had been in full force at that time, would Bretton Woods have had any power whatsoever to prevent those developments in the United States? I think practically every hon member of this committee will have to agree it would not have had any power. It must be obvious that Bretton Woods would have been useless as a remedial or protective measure against that situation.
What resulted? The United States economy was so powerful, it filled such a tremendous place in the world's economy, that the minute this terrible depression developed in the United States it was able to throw out of gear the economies of all other countries. What happened in Great Britain was the natural result of what happened in the United States. Great Britain began to use exchange controls, currency regulations and all that kind of thing to protect herself in some measure against the condition of the United States.
Let me give a simple illustration. The prices of primary commodities fell in the United States, commodities such as beef. If beef had been shipped to England in 1931 or 1932 at the prices prevailing in the United States, unquestionably it would have displaced British beef and upset the whole economy .as far as agriculture in Great Britain was concerned. The only possible means by which Great Britain could prevent that sort of thing was some sort of exchange restriction or some sort of tariff or some sort of quota or some sort of anti-dumping measure. If , Bretton
[Mr. Macdonnell.J
Woods had been in operation at that time she would have been denied the privilege of using all those.	, \
What good would Bretton Woods have been? No good at all. It must be obvious to every member of the committee how completely fallacious is the reasoning that the minister has used here, or that the experts who wrote that speech have used in that particular passage. I am not reflecting on the minister at all, and L want hon. members to understand that. The marvel to me is that the man can live with the amount of work he has had to do. I am positively amazed that he can live. I am astounded that his health has not been smashed all to smithereens long ago because of the terrific pressure of work that is on him.
Of course he has to get the best expert advice he can in preparing his speech. That is a foregone conclusion. He is different from us. I wish to relieve the minister of complete responsibility. How in the world can the Minister of Finance be so well informed on everything that he can do every kind of work that is to be done? He must depend on experts. One of the main lines that this group has followed and is following is that those experts are wrong and, consequently, the minister, following the advice of the experts, and this house, following slavishly and docilely the advice of the minister, will be wrong. It becomes the duty of this house to be critical in the highest degree of the recommendations of these experts. That is not necessarily a reflection on the experts; it is a reflection probably on the training which they have had and which has not equipped them to cope with new situations. No one ever had to face such a depression as the great depression until it came along and the experts did not know how to deal with it.

How could they be expected to tell all about the causes? We must realize that we are dealing with fallible men, men with limitations. The whole argument of Social Credit is to advocate that we should in the name of reason and common sense act like men and not accept slavishly every suggestion which is offered by the minister on the advice of his experts. Let us try to find out something about the problem ourselves, so that we may be intelligent in our own conclusions. The fallacy in the passage which I have indicated must be completely obvious to every single member of the committee.
Let me go a little bit further to show that this fallacy upon which the government is working is deep seated. The first definite

Bretton Woods Agreements
pronouncement which the government made, so far as I know, on the question of Bretton Woods was made in a white paper called Employment and Income which was presented to the house in April, 1945, by the Minister of Reconstruction. May I suggest to hon. members that they take that white paper and turn to page 7 and read what is said regarding Bretton Woods and Dumbarton Oaks. I quote as follows:
Having regard to the widespread character of our trade, the government attaches special importance also to the reconstruction of multilateral trade on a permanent basis and arrangements under which the proceeds of our exports may be spent wherever we desire to obtain our imports.
With that no one can quarrel.
It is with these objects in mind that the government has participated in the development of the plans for the international monetary fund and the united nations bank of reconstruction and development on which agreement among experts was reached at Bretton Woods in July last.
I am not questioning that the government entered into the Bretton Woods agreement with full sincerity and actually believed that the Bretton Woods agreement would constitute a remedy or provide remedial action in the situation. What follows is significant in connection with our discussion:
The monetary fund plan would assure comparative stability of exchange rates and, where change was desirable, would substitute for competitive depreciation of exchanges an orderly proce'ss of change following international consultation.
That is all right, but it is a bit general to be of any value. Notice this next sentence, which reads:
It would outlaw the discriminatory currency practices which turned trade into economic warfare.
May I pause to point out to the members of the committee that right there the fundamental fallacy creeps in. The statement is positively made that it was the currency practices which brought on economic warfare, when as a matter of fact it was the economic warfare resulting from the depression which produced the currency practices. That is obvious. Just as soon as prices fell in the United States and she had to dump her goods and take other protective measures, the economic warfare resulted which produced these currency practices. That is abundantly obvious. Yet this statement is made by the experts, a statement which is an absolute and unquestionable fallacy. May I read it again:
It would outlaw the discriminatory currency practices which turned trade into economic warfare. When it was fully in operation, it would
assure the convertibility of the proceeds of our sales abroad into whatever currencies we required for our current needs.
No one will quarrel particularly with that statement. It goes on:
It would give to each member country for the purposes of its current balance of payments an assured, though limited, line of credit to serve as a buttress to policies directed >to the expansion of employment.
I do not need to read the next two paragraphs but I feel that if I do not, somebody will say that I am distorting by quoting paragraphs out of their context. So, if the committee will permit me, I will read the next two paragraphs, just to be completely fair to the writer of this article:
The regular transfer of capital from surplus to deficit countries for purposes of reconstruction and development is essential to the expansion and stability of international trade. The Bank of Reconstruction and Development would provide through an international institution for a needed revival of international investment.
I doubt that. I doubt whether the existence of the international bank and international stabilization fund would have caused those lenders in the United States to continue lending in 1928-29 when they began to realize that they could not. get their money back because the United States had a tariff that would prevent imports from coming in to pay for the interest on the loans, much less the loans themselves, as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario said. Does anyone imagine that United States public opinion as it is at the present time would allow the administration in that country to lower their tariffs sufficiently to allow goods to come in to compete with United States goods? It just is not common sense. So you see once more the fundamental fallacy of that whole attitude, the fundamental and inexcusable error and fallacy. It goes on:
In the interest of Canadian and world prosperity and of peaceful collaboration among nations, the government endorses these plans and hopes that parliament will in due_ course approve the draff agreements. In reaching this view, the government is mindful of the pos-sibity that Canada might, as a member of both institutions, occupy the position of a "creditor" nation.
I am deeply sorry, Mr. Chairman, that that statement was made. It is correct but it means this, as the member for Acadia so well pointed out the other day. The thing which destroys confidence, the thing which ruins the lives of nations is this, that they have goods thrown on to their markets by dumping, export subsidies and all that, which completely puts out of business their industries and throws men on the street as unemployed. That is the trouble. It is the fact that they have

It is our opinion that this whole proposal is a pernicious one, and we think that the committee should give it most earnest consideration before even considering such a thing as adopting it.
At one time in my remarks I was pointing out the fundamental fallacy which is to be found in the government's position in the matter. I quoted a passage from the speech of the Minister of Finance, and also referred to a statement which is found in the white paper called Employment and Income, which was presented to the house in April, 1945, by the Minister of Reconstruction, Then I was about to read a passage from the speech of Henry Morgenthau, Junior, delivered to the delegates at Bretton Woods, in their closing plenary session in July, 1944. My object in reading this passage was to give the committee the background of the whole question, and to help show the attitude of the United States to the whole situation.
Before reading this passage may I point out once more in different language that there simply is no use in trying to apply what is supposed to be a cure or a remedy for a malady the nature of which we have not discovered. There is no earthly use, for example, in trying to prescribe a cure for the pimples of smallpox, until one finds out what is the cause of smallpox. If you wish to cure smallpox, you find out the cause, and then attack that cause: The same applies' to great international problems. We will grant that the world is suffering from a malady, and that it was' suffering from that malady as far back as 1925. The Bretton Woods proposal is supposed to be an important part of the remedy for that malady. We maintain that it has nothing whatsoever to do with the remedy for the malady. The malady must be remedied by measures altogether different from anything found in Bretton Woods.
May I now read the passage from Henry Morgenthau, Junior, where he says:
This is the alternative-
The alternative to Bretton Woods-
-to the desperate tactics of the past-competitive currency depreciation, excessive tariff barriers, uneconomic barter deals, multiple currency practices and unnecessary exchange restrictions-by which governments vainly sought to maintain employment and uphold diving standards. In the final analysis, these tactics only succeeded in contributing to world wide depression and even war. The international fund agreed upon at Bretton Woods will help remedy this situation.
He says it will help to remedy the situation. He does not maintain that it will be a complete remedy. We will grant that. But I wish to concentrate the attention of members of the committee on that second to last sentence, where he says-
In the final analysis, these tactics only succeeded in contributing to world-wide depression and even war.

The need of the situation to-day is distribution of goods internally and internationally. As the hon. member will recall, the hon. member for Acadia the other day asked the minister if he was prepared to bring about- a complete effective demand in Canada for Canada's production. Suppose Canada had twelve billion dollars' worth of production in a year after the war. The maximum need would be twelve billion dollars' worth of purchasing power in Canada available to buy that production. If Canadian people did not wish to buy all the production of Canada's wheat, for example, that surplus could be traded for bananas or other things w'hich Canadians need, and Canadians would be able to buy those goods when they arrived. Do I make that quite clear to the hon. gentleman?
I was pointing out the causes of the depression. Number one was the cessation of foreign lending. I thank the hon. member for asking me that question. I welcome questions of that kind from any member in the house, because Social Crediters are not condemning this proposal without offering an alternative. They condemn this proposal, and they condemn the whole present orthodox financial system, on the ground that it is absolutely impossible for it to distribute the goods of the world and to eliminate competitive trade, which means economic warfare, which in turn means military warfare in the end.
The second step toward the bringing on of the depression was the raising of the rediscount rate by the federal reserve board. The minute the rediscount rate was raised by the federal reserve board the banks were unable to obtain money as easily upon which to base loans for large investments, including security on speculations. That meant there was retraction of money immediately all over the country. That was the second step in the bringing on of the depression.

The third step was the loss of confidence in securities by the speculators. Those who were ready to pay large sums for mining stocks, gold stocks and stocks of lumber mills and all that kind of thing began to be afraid because they said,' "We may lose." They then began to hesitate and began to try to sell., which immediately brought on the depression, and the consequence was a complete collapse of the 'economy of the country.
The fourth step was the calling of loans. The withdrawing of circulating medium naturally resulted all over the country, because the lending policy of the banks is intimately bound up with the lending policy of the banks to those who wish to deal in securities. Does the hon. member get that?
The fifth step was the fall of prices which naturally resulted from a withdrawal of purchasing power throughout the country. I was speaking from memory when I mentioned this a while ago, but I think I am right. According to Irving Fisher, a great economist, in his book called "A Hundred Per Cent Money", eight billion of the twenty-three billion dollars in circulation in the United States in 1929 were withdrawn, and this brought on a fall in prices and in values all over the United States.

I think I could count them pretty well with the' fingers of one hand. We have reached the stage where if we are to have peace; if we are to have that measure of cooperation that will bring about prosperity, not only for ourselves but for others, we must be ready to give up a great deal of our national sovereignty. Indeed that is the way world progress has been made. Not only have people given up things, but privileges have been taken away from sections or from groups in order that those privileges might be extended to even larger numbers of people. That is the way democracy has developed in nations; and that is the way it must develop in the international sphere.
I consider such a statement as that, in face of the actual conditions of the world, nothing short of criminal lunacy. There are only two or three nations that have preserved their national sovereignty, of which Canada is one, thank God 1 It is only in those nations where national sovereignty has been maintained that the people can meet in their parliaments and exercise freedom of speech. Let me remind hon. members of what the British secretary for foreign affairs said recently in the parliament at Westminster. But first let me remind hon. members of the Atlantic charter. The third has been to tax the middle class so as to demoralize them by fear and reduce them to servitude and impotence. I am not criticizing Keynes, but I am saying that a teacher who changes virtually overnight in some of his cardinal teachings, I would hesitate to quote personally as an authority to-day as readily as I would before I read that book, and I say this without derogating at all from his right to change his mind. I put that on record because some members might suggest that the statement I made the other day regarding Mr. Dunning was not quite correct.

In all fairness to Doctor Clark I think I should put his words on Hansard, as recorded in the report of the special committee on reconstruction and re'establishment dated Wednesday, March 8, 1944. Perhaps Doctor Clark would like to say whether he agrees with the proposals put forward by the London chamber of commerce? No doubt Doctor Clark has made a study of those proposals.

I do not think I should be asked to go on with the London chamber of commerce programme this morning. The next opportunity I had to speak with him was when I accidentally met him in the corridor. I asked him his attitude regarding the London chamber of commerce, and it was that which I put on record. Now to get on with the question of the creditor nation Doctor Clark said this:
Mr. Quelch also made a point about the difference in the treatment between debtor and creditor countries under the plans, suggesting

that the treatment of debtor countries was far more strict and mandatary than in the case of the creditor countries. I do not think -that is really a fair reading of the three plans. I think all three plans recognize very clearly and emphasize very strongly the obligation that the creditor country is under to do the things that will get it out of -that chronic creditor position [DOT]and enable the world really to function as a whole. In the case of the creditor countries I might read very briefly what I said in this -address about what is provided in respect to creditor countries.
All three plans recognize that surplus countries may be equally responsible with deficit countries for creating disequilibria in international exchange. To illustrate the general -application of the plans to surplus countries, let me take the major provisions of the Canadian plan. When the union's operations have resulted in net sales of the currency of any member to the extent of 75 per cent of its quota, the union may attempt to arrange with that country a programme of capital investment or securities repatriation in order to increase -its reserves of the currency in question. When net sales of a currency have reached 85 per cent of a country's quota, -the union has the authority -and the duty to render to that country a report analysing the causes of -the depletion of its holdings of the particular currency and making recommendations in regard to monetary and fiscal policies, exchange rate, commercial policy, and -international investment, believed to be appropriate in order to restore the equilibrium of the international balances of the country concerned. The union has also the right to enter into arrangements with any country to borrow additional supplies of its currency on mutually satisfactory terms, and. when the hoard believes that the anticipated demand for any currency may soon exhaust the union's holdings, it is required to propose a method for the equitable distribution of the scarce currency together with suggestions for helping to equate the anticipated demand and supply. When it finds it necessary thus to ration a scarce currency the board is required to reexamine prevailing exchange rates and recommend such changes as it may believe appropriate to the changed circumstances.	,
Might I interject here that the question of scarce currency is dealt with in article 7 of the Bretton Woods agreement. He goes on to say:
True, several of the provisions I have read -are, as Mr. Queleh says, of an advisory character; hut if the fund had the power to enforce on a creditor country all these measures or had other equally drastic powers. I am afraid Mr. Queleh would say that we were suggesting a plan which too greatly impaired the national sovereignty of a country. So you could easily go too far in that direction, and I think what is provided for in these plans goes much farther than anything that has ever been done in the past to solve the problem of the creditor country, to bring the creditor country to a realization of what it must do if it is going to solve its own problems and not be a drag on the prosperity of the world.
The provisions are largely in the category of an advisory nature. He wants to know whether I would expect them to suggest that f\lr. Queleh.]

We have no right to impose conditions on the debtor nation and let the creditor nation go scot-free, but should recognize that they both should have a mutual obligation to try to balance their trade. I replied to Doctor Clark in this way:
Before we adjourn I would like to take up the question of impairing the sovereignty of a nation, because I agree entirely with Doctor Clark on -that point. To my mind one of the main objections to these proposals is due to the fact -that while they do not intend to impair the sovereignty of a creditor nation, they do so in the case of a debtor nation, and I say a creditor nation would be largely to blame because if the creditor nation refused to buy a debtor nation's goods the debtor nation is at its mercy.
Doctor Clark agrees that foreign investment is not a solution, that it just tides over the period of unemployment for the time being, that it cannot be considered a longterm solution.
I should like to quote a statement from the London Economist to show that people who have studied this question generally agree that foreign investment is not a solution but merely a temporary expedient. The London Economist of January 22, 1944. says:
Loans, unless the word is to be a euphemism for charity can never be a permanent solution. Interest has to be paid on that and in due course they have to be repaid. The world has tried once before to buttress the metallic system and the results do not encourage repetition of the experiment, especially as it would have to be a larger programme.
That is just what we are proposing to do under the Bretton Woods agreement.
In connection with the international stabilization of currency, I should like to show that Maynard Keynes recognizes the fact that the creditor nation has a responsibility, and he actually went so far as to say- that if a creditor nation refused to accept imports its credit should be cancelled. I quote from section 3, page 10, of this pamphlet on the international stabilization of currency:
It is not contemplated that either the debit or the credit balance of an individual country ought to exceed a certain maximum-let us say, its quota. In the case of debit balances -this maximum has been made a rigid one, and, indeed, counter-measures are called for long before the maximum is reached. In the case of credit balances no rigid maximum has been proposed. For the appropriate provision might be to require the eventual cancellation or compulsory investment of persistent bancor credit balances accumulating in excess of a member's quota.
I repeat that phrase: "the appropriate provision might be to require the eventual cancellation."

Just to show that that line of thought has been followed by many other people besides Ive3'nes, I should like to quote a recommendation of the London chamber of commerce on this proposal. So that there may be no mis. understanding may I say that I have here two pamphlets, one of the report of the London chamber of commerce on "General Principles of a Post-war Economy", and the other a pamphlet entitled "A Twentieth Century Economic System," on the front page of which I read this:
The author has decided to remain anonymous, in the hope that his fellow citizens will insist, on this occasion, on doing their own thinking, and will consider these proposals on their merits, uninfluenced by the names and reputations of the protagonists on either side.
The reason I link these two together is because on page 11, section 27, of the London chamber of commerce report, I find this:
The chamber, having considered whether there is any system which would achieve, wholly or partially, the solution of all the above problems, generally accepts the principles laid down in "A Twentieth Century Economic System," especially in respect of blocked credits for the payment of international obligations.
I had better quote a paragraph from "A Twentieth Centuiy Economic System" dealing with this very question. It gives an explanation of bilateral trade on page 25, and then goes on to say:
The above is a simple example of bilateral trade, but multilateral trade could be provided for by the exchange controls of the participating nations having representatives at an international exchange where blocked credits in one country could be exchanged for those in another at the conventionally fixed exchange rates: the primary responsibility for establishing a contra account, by importing from the country to which a sale had been made, would remain with the exporting country. If it did not wish to do so that would be its affair and not that of the importing country, which would have done its part by establishing the necessary credit. The importing country would be entitled to cancel the credit, under a statute of limitations, if it were not used within seven years. The principle is that with which we are all familiar in internal trading: if you have a credit with a shop, you cannot take it out in cash but you clear it when you take goods.
A further comment regarding international exchange is shown at the bottom of the page. Perhaps I had better quote it, because several hon. members have the idea in their heads that we advocate bilateral trade. We have never advocated bilateral trade. We realize the benefits of multilateral trade; but we do feel this, that when a nation establishes a credit with another nation it should be under some obligation to see that that credit is cleared. Therefore, if we establish a credit with France, and want to buy goods from Germany. if Germany is willing to take goods from
France there is no reason why we cannot take goods from Germany and Germany can take goods from France. Here is a quotation indicating how goods could be traded on an international exchange:
The international exchange would be in no sense an international bank nor would it be the body with which all the nations would hold their debits and credits. Psychologically it is important that each nation should know in which countries it has uneancelled credits, so that it may take steps to clear those credits either by taking more imports or by restricting its exports to them. The responsibility which this scheme places squarely upon each nation to keep its own imports and exports in equilibrium, must in no circumstances be transferred to a central international clearing bank. If a central international bank were entrusted with this task instead of each nation being free to solve its own domestic problem in its own way, we should once more be back to the old condition of financial war to control a central monetary authority which, in its turn, would control the domestic affairs of so-called independent nations. In practice, such a system of central international monetary control means that whilst effective pressure cannot be put upon the strong creditor nations _ to take payment in goods against their wishes, great pressure can be brought to bear upon the weak debtor nations to lower their prices in an attempt to force their goods over the tariffs of creditors unwilling to receive payment in the only way open to the debtor, namely in goods.
The hon member for Rosthern interrupted when I was speaking on Saturday and tried to give the house the impression that provision was made in the Bretton Woods agreement for putting a very great deal of pressure on a creditor nation; and really, when I read his remarks in Hansard I was amazed that he would make a statement of that kind, because after all be did go to Bretton Woods, and therefore he should know what he is talking about. Where he got' this statement I do not know, because it certainly is not in the Bretton Woods agreement. Let me quote what he said-I am sorry the hon. member is not in his place at the moment-as reported in Hansard, at purge 3146:
The fundamental basis of this organization is that if a currency becomes scarce then the country whose currency has become scarce will be advised by the officials of the fund that they must take steps to -enable other countries to sell their goods in the country of the scarce currency, and they would advise that country that they must be prepared to correct that fundamental unbalance of trade. The whole basis of this agreement is designed to promote understanding between countries in order to permit balanced trade and the keeping up of high standards of living in all countries.
It is all very well to say that that is the understanding; but when you use the word "must",
I think one would assume there should be something definite about that in the agreement itself. I would, however, invite hon. members
Bretton Woods Agreements

to note what article VII which deals with the question of scarce currencies, really says in regard to relationship with creditor countries. There is no compulsion, with the exception that they must be ready to sell their currency for gold. That is the only compulsion in the whole thing. I am quoting from article VII in order to show how far afield from reality the hon. member for Rosthern had got when he said that they must do this and they must do that:
If the fund finds that a general scarcity of a particular currency is developing, the fund may so inform members and may issue a report setting forth the causes of the scarcity and containing recommendations designed to bring it to an end.
That is the furthest they go. They issue a report containing recommendations; but for some reason or another the hon. member for Rosthern jumps to the conclusion that they must do this or they must do that. I continue to quote:
A representative of the member whose currency is involved shall participate in the preparation of the report.
Then, quoting from section 2 of the same article:
The fund may, if it deems such action appropriate to replenish its holdings of any member's currency, take either or both of the following steps':
(i) Propose to the member that, on terms and conditions agreed between the fund and the member, the latter lend its currency to the fund or that, with the approval of the member, the fund borrow such currency from some other source either within or outside the territories of the member, but-
Here is the important point:
-no member shall be under any obligation to make such loans to the fund . . .
They cannot even compel a creditor nation to lend its currency or to approve the borrowing of its currency by the fund from any other source. The only reference to compulsion is in subparagraph (ii), which states that the fund may:
. . . require the member to sell its currency to the fund for gold.
Apparently the aim of the creditor country is to get as much gold as it can; I do not think it is putting much compulsion on the creditor nation to say that it must accept gold in return for its currency. What is lacking there is that there is no provision whereby the creditor nation can assist the debtor nation by enabling it to pay in the only way it can, namely by accepting its goods and services. Under this system and under the gold standard the results are the same. When a nation has an unfavourable balance of trade, it has either to meet the unbalance of trade by gold, if it cannot get
[Mr. Quvlch.l
any currency by selling goods, or to accept a loan, and if it has to accept a loan, after a period of time the creditor nation will just be buying up its capital assets.

There is another point here. Not only does it not penalize a creditor nation, but it actually rewards the creditor nation for being such and penalizes the debtor nation for being a debtor nation still further, beyond an increase of interest rates; because if we look_ up the question of voting, referred to in section 5 of article XII, we find out how the votes are apportioned between the various members. I read section 5 on this point:
V oting.
(a)	Each member shall have two hundred and fifty votes plus one additional vote for each part of its quota equivalent to one hundred thousand United States dollars.
(b)	Whenever voting is required under article V, section 4 or 5, each member shall have the number of votes to which it is entitled under (a) above, adjusted:
(i)	by the addition of one vote for the equivalent of each four hundred thousand United States dollars of net sales of its currency up to the date -when the vote is taken, or
(ii)	by the subtraction of one vote for the equivalent of each four hundred thousand United States dollars of its net purchases of the currencies of other members up to the date when the vote is taken.
So we find that under that section the further into debt a nation gets, the less is its voting power; the greater creditor a nation becomes, the greater the amount of loans made by a creditor nation, the greater the number of its votes becomes. Therefore, after a period of time you find a great change in the voting strength. You will find that creditor nations are gradually accumulating more and more votes and debtor nations are getting fewer and fewer; and when you think of the possibilities of the future, the amount of money which in all probability the United States, for example, will be lending, you can see that the voting power of that country will be tremendously increased. No doubt the government has given some consideration to the question I am about to put to the minister. That is just a matter of opinion; it is not self-evident. I know all through the years the Social Credit party have argued that this would have happened in time of peace, but in time of peace you have a different set of conditions from those that exist in time of war. In time of war you have a unified national purpose, and it does not deter industrial or agricultural activity at all for the government to spend large sums of money, put up taxes, increase the credit and to some extent inflate, because there has been some degree of inflation during the war. That does not alarm or retard investment and enterprise. But when you do not have that set of conditions that may not be the result. Therefore you have various schools of thought as to the best means to adopt to get all your people working with fair incomes. The C.C.F. has one view. They think it is a matter of the government taking over at least quite a lot of the big business of the country, that if you take it out of private hands you are more likely to get full employment. The Social Credit party I think believe that the application of the monetary remedy is sufficient of itself.
Those are the questions, and they are questions as to which there is a great difference of opinion. I do not think this is the proper ' occasion for us to get into a debate, which can be very far-reaching, as to what is the best programme to adopt to keep all your people gainfully employed. Certainly we have not been silent in the last twelve months as. to the means we are seeking to adopt or aiming to adopt. They are set out in the white paper on reconstruction on "Employment and Income," and they were fully publicized during the election campaign, and in speeches since that time. We would propose to do it by a variety of steps, not by one alone.

Unless the creditor nation were prepared to change their policy to one of expansion; unless they were willing to develop an expansionist policy internally, why do they have to wait until currency is scarce before they do that?
We might as well face the fact that the greatest menace in the world to-day is the policy of the United States in trying to export its unemployment problem upon the world. I cannot see that this will help the situation. It would just mean that the exports from the United States would be reduced, while the standard of living would be reduced in the debtor nations. When we establish a credit in another country by selling it goods we have a definite responsibility to accept goods in payment, or at least to provide that if we take goods from another country that pountry will utilize the credit which we have established in the former country. Surely it is not a question of sovereignty; it is a question of fair and square dealing. I would point out that the provision which the minister has read would not operate if a creditor nation sold unlimited sums of its currency for gold. Then the debtor countries could obtain the currency which the creditor country sold, and they would still be going steadily further into debt. By the creditor countries selling their currency for gold the debtor countries would obtain currency from the fund, but they would go further into debt. I do not understand why anybody would advocate that. Keynes recognized the danger and so did the London chamber of commerce. I think we all recognize the danger of the creditor nation not being under obligation to accept payment in goods. I cannot understand why that provision is not in the Bretton Woods agreement, whilst it was not in the Morgenthau plan, the Keynes plan or the Canadian plan. I am speaking from memory; I believe they provided for a slight tax upon the creditor nation. Under this plan there is absolutely no pressure on the creditor nation apart from the two sections which the minister read, and that is a slight pressure.
There are one or two points with which I should like the minister to deal. I think he will realize that it is something that should be dealt with.

Again I quote from a man who the minister will admit is quite an authority- Sir Charles" Morgan-Webb. He has this to say:
Britain need have no fear for the revival of her export industries if the entanglement of Bretton Woods can be avoided, and if her overseas pounds sterling are kept off a gold basis. As long as they are redeemable in goods, they provide an expansive currency capable of meeting all the requirements of an expanding world trade. But if they are made redeemable in old they become a deadweight deflationary urden that can never be redeemed. The linking of the war debts of the first world war to the capricious medium of gold inevitably made them unpayable. The linking of the present overseas cash debts owing by Britain to gold, as proposed at Bretton Woods, will transform them from an obligation to redeem them in exports into an unpayable obligation to redeem them in gold. As they stand, they are payable in British exports. Transformed into gold obligations,^ they will fulfil the expectations of American high finance, and drive Britain into default.
As soon as Britain got into a position where she had exceeded her quota by 200 per cent, the only way this scarce currency could be obtained would be for gold, and Britain would be forced still further into debt. A man of this writer's standing would not make such a statefnent as I have quoted without ample justification.

Maynard Keynes, in his book "International Stabilization of Currency," makes it clear that he is not keen about the idea of gold entering into the scheme, but he points out that it would no doubt be impossible to get the United States to agree to any programme that did not bring gold into the picture. He makes that clear. He points out that nations are agreeing because of the insistence of the United States. Appeasement in the past has always failed. We got ourselves in a mess from 1935 on as a result of trying to appease others. We shall get nowhere now, I suggest, by trying to appease the United States at this time. In doing so we are only laying up trouble for ourselves in the future, and I am quite satisfied that the result is bound to be international friction. The minister asks me, will it be detrimental to Canada? I say, so far as our trading is concerned, no; but so far as helping to destroy peace in the world, I say definitely yes. I would remind the minister that these experts and international financiers, in whom apparently he has such faith, have been harsh taskmasters in the past. I have here a copy of what'occurred. I do not think I need to read from it, but I would remind the minister what happened when the Niemeyer mission went to Australia in 1939. This shows the kind of treatment a nation gets when it places itself in the position outlined by section eight of article V. This is the treatment it will get from Otto Niemeyer. Perhaps it is just as well for me to put this on the record. Hon. members will find it written in a book,
by J. T. Lang, leader of the Labour party in New South W'ales. The book is entitled "Why I Fight":
The mission consisted of Sir Otto Niemeyer, a representative of the bank who had acted in the similar capacity of official assignee in the case of many European countries; Professor T. E. Gregory, of the London school of economics and Mr. R. N. Kershaw, former Australian Rhodes scholar, designated as "liaison officer".
Then I quote.
Extracts from Sir Otto's address make interesting reading after an interval of four years: "It is a serious problem," he said, "the practical solution of which is not rendered any easier by the natural optimism of the Australian. So long as it is generally believed in Australia that there is an unlimited market abroad for Australian goods, and that something will turn up, it will be difficult to face the realities of the position."
Australia had an unfavourable balance of trade. Sir Otto points out that they had a surplus of goods, but they are in difficulties not because of scarcity of goods, but because they could not get creditor nations to lake those goods. Submissively the premiers carried a series of resolutions at the dictation of Sir Otto, declaring:

That is the kind of difficulty you get into when you put yourself under the dictatorship of a certain kind of authority. bers of tbe fund shall be submitted to the executive directors for their decision. If the question particularly affects any member not entitled to appoint an executive director it shall be entitled to representation in accordance with article XI, section 3 (j).

From that I gather that in the normal course matters of disagreement would be settled by the executive directors or the board of governors, and that if a member felt it was unjustly treated it might withdraw from the fund. I think it is quite obvious
that it cannot become one, due to the fact that it is practically a law unto itself. How could it possibly come under the united nations charter when you have article IX, which gives immunities and privileges as follows:
To enable the fund to fulfil the functions with which it is entrusted, the status, immunities and privileges set forth in this article shall he accorded to the fund in the territories of each member.
The fund shall possess full juridical personality, and, in particular, the capacity:
(i)	to contract;
(ii)	to acquire and dispose of immovable and movable property;
(iii)	to institute legal proceedings.
Mind you the fund can institute legal proceedings .against anyone, but no one can institute legal proceedings against the fund. It is immune from all legal action.
The fund, its property and its assets, wherever located and by whomsoever held, shall enjoy immunity from every form of judicial process except to the extent that it expressly waives its immunity for the purpose of any proceedings or by the terms of any contract.
Property and assets of the fund, wherever located and by whomsoever held, shall be immune from search, requisition, confiscation, expropriation or any other form of seizure by executive or legislative action.
The archives of the fund shall be inviolable.
To the extent necessary to carry out the operations provided for in this agreement, all property and assets of the fund shall be free from restrictions, regulations, controls and moratoria of any nature.
It is to be free of all regulation and restriction within any country in the world; yet we are seriously giving consideration to setting up a body which is to be above al! laws and all governments and apparently even above the international court of justice. The only provision is that arbitration may be carried out by a member of the fund, the fund itself and a third person appointed by the court of international justice, but no legal action can be taken against the fund. Surely in view of the fact that we are setting up an international court of justice a nation should have the right, to take legal action against the fund before that- international court. Does the minister not. agree that there should be some possibility of action in that regard, and that a nation should be allowed to take legal proceedings against the fund? speechtext:
Before six o'clock the hon. member for Acadia had been discussing certain features of the final act of the Bretton Woods agreement. He called the attention of the committee to article IX, which refers to status, immunities and privileges.
Perhaps hon. members may think that we in this corner of the chamber seem to be particularly incensed at this agreement; but
Bretton Woods Agreements

when attention is called to some of the tremendous powers granted to this central organization, we have indeed reason to be alarmed.
In the matter of immunities, the hon. member for Acadia has already pointed out to the committee that ,the fund is here personalized, according to section 2, which states:
The fund shall possess full juridical personality and, in particular, the capacity . . .
And so on. We must consider that they have almost all power, and that no other organization, no other nation and no other sovereign power have, the right to sue them In other words, no nation has any recourse, no redress, when once those in charge of the fund have made a decision. That is an alarming thing.
May I call the attention of the committee to some other sections under this article, so that hon. members may see the extent to which we are handing over authority and power to this fund, without having any right of redress whatsoever, even as a nation. In section 8 we find the heading "Immunities and privileges of officers and employees". The section states:	'
AH governors, executive directors, alternates, officers and employees of the fund
(i)	shall be immune from legal process with respect to acts performed by them in their official capacity except when the fund waives this immunity.
I a.m not so much concerned about that clause, because perhaps an individual cannot be permitted to be sued, if it is the decision of the entire body. But look at the next clause:
(ii)	not being local nationals, shall be granted the' same immunities from immigration restrictions, alien registration requirements and national service obligations and the same facilities as regards exchange restrictions as are accorded by members to the representatives, officials, and employees of comparable rank ot other members.
I hope I understand that. Perhaps I do not; but it appears to me that you have men in control of this fund who can travel all over the world, and that we, as a nation, cannot even ask what right they have here. That seems to me to be tremendously irregular.
I am often reminded that when some visitor goes to the United States, our good neighbour to the south, very often an hon. member will rise here and ask if the government has taken any action to invite such person to this country. That has been done on a number of occasions. When that is done I often feel like asking myself, "Well, since when do some of these other nations rise in their legislative assemblies and ask if the government have invited any of our men to look over what they may have to show?"
[Mr. Hansell.l
Here is a. section under which these people may come and go as they wish. That seems strange to me. Are we to permit it? If we sign the agreement it looks as though we will.
Paragraph (iii) says:
(iii)	shall be granted the same treatment in respect of travelling facilities as is accorded by members to representatives, officials and employees of comparable rank of other members.
If I have not got that right, I would ask the minister to say where I am wrong.
But one of the most startling sections of all, to my mind, is section 10. I want the minister to read that. I suppose he has already done so, but I suggest that he should refresh his memory. The title of that section is "Application of article," and it begins in this way:
Each member shall take such action . . .
"each member"; that is, each nation which signs the agreement and becomes a part of the whole. Each member, each nation, shall take such action. It does not say "may" take such action. "Shall" seems to me to be obligatory. It states:
Each member shall take such action as is necessary in its own territories for the purpose of making effeotive in terms of its own law the principles set forth in this article and shall in-^ form the fund of the detailed action, which it* has taken.
It seems to me that if Canada signs this article we are signing away our right over certain of our own laws and our own legislative powers, and that the moment we sign the agreement we must then readjust any legislation on our statute books that' may, in any way, hinder the smooth functioning of this fund.
To me that is strange language. It - is strange if we- cannot be master of our own legislation. It means that if we have on our statute books legislation which is considered in the interest of our nation but is found to conflict with the operations of this fund, as part of the agreement we are forced to change our law. We are forced to change our laws so that we can. be told by this outside power what to do. If that is not the right interpretation of this section I want the minister to tell me what is wrong with it. We have heard a good deal about sovereign rights, which I believe in, but surely it is going too far toward giving away our sovereign rights when we give some other body the right to say what legislation we should have and to permit that outside power to say that -we can or cannot have this or that legislation.
The other day we were asked to give power to our own government to control certain matters. What are we being asked to do here? If our government goes too far we

Bretton Woods Agreements
can. check them; we have some recourse in this parliament; but when this is done we are giving away our sovereign rights and power to an outside authority with regard to certain legislation. We shall have no control over that power, and I think that is a serious matter. I do not think we can be blamed for being as incensed as we are in a matter of this kind.

May I read from page 17 of the act which was distributed in the house. The minister read portions of it before the dinner recess. I am going to read the recommendations, so that tho'se who read Hansard will know just exactly what is here. They read as follows:
Whereas, in article I of the articles of agreement of the international monetary fund it is stated that' one of the principal purposes of the fund is to facilitate the expansion and balanced
growth of international trade, and to contribute thereby to the promotion and maintenance of high levels of employment and real income and to the development of the productive resources of all members as primary objectives of economic policy;	_
Whereas, it is recognized that the complete attainment of this and other purposes and objectives stated in the agreement cannot be achieved through the instrumentality of the fund alone; therefore
The united nations monetary and financial conference recommends:
To the participating governments that, in addition to implementing the specific monetary and financial measures which were the subject of this conference, they seek, with a view to creating in the field of international economic relations conditions necessary for the attainment of the purposes of the fund and of the broader primary objectives of economic policy, to reach agreement as soon as possible on ways and means whereby they may best:

(4)	facilitate by cooperatitve effort the harmonization of national policies of member states designed to promote and maintain high levels of ^employment and progressively rising standards of living.
If those four recommendations could be implemented they would simply attain the promised land so far as social crediters are concerned. If we could only learn how to attain those objectives all would be well. The minister must have given this a good deal of attention, and surely the experts who went down there so nobly and performed so ably for twenty-two days and did this wonderful thing in drafting the Bretton Woods agreement, must have reported to him something about this. Why was this matter not taken care of before Bretton Woods was drafted? Obviously the harness was got before either the cart or the horse. We often hear of that cart being brought out before the horse; but here the harness has been brought in before the cart and before the horse. The harness is all ready to bind us hand and foot, but we

If a nation is to protect its economy at all, tariffs wall have to come in to a certain extent and exchange controls and quotas will have to come in, and, in fact, every other kind of protective device which the nations have, had to employ in the past; otherwise something else must come in to take the place of that protection. The fundamental position which social crediters take and which new economists generally take is that there must be a distribution of goods in the world under a system which will render it possible to aid nations like Belgium so that they will not have to impose these restrictions. If we could find a single hint anywhere in all the deliberations of all committees which are at work to-day, that there is any idea in their minds as to how that distribution of goods could be brought about, we would be reassured; but I cannot find any sign of that;
I cannot find a hint of it. So that I say. as far as I can see, unless something is explained more than has been explained up to the present time, this first recommendation is just pure piffle and does not have any effect at all. It talks of reducing the obstacles to international trade, at the same time that everybody knows perfectly well that they cannot be reduced without the destruction of the world's weaker economies. If they cannot be replaced without the destruction of those weaker economies, then certainly the cause of war is not being removed, and to bring in Bretton Woods and make it still more difficult for them to protect their economies is simply to aggravate the situation. Surely that must

be plain to every hon. member in the committee. What we are arguing is that there is in Bretton Woods no solution of the problem. The problem is international trade war, and the devices the nations have adopted to protect themselves are the devices which we are supposed to remove, without giving them any means whereby they can remove the need for protection. There is the difficulty. If the minister can give us any reassurance on that matter we should like to have it.
May I just illustrate this for the committee, to give us something to put our teeth into. In the 1930's Japan managed by a device which she was using to bring down the price of her goods for export. I have read this, although I am speaking entirely from memory, that Japan enabled herself to offer a bicycle for S5.75 for which we would charge $50 here in Canada. If we had not adopted a method of practical embargo, of absolute exclusion against Japan, we people in Canada and the United States, with all our productive potential, would have found ourselves buying Japanese goods, and the first thing we knew our people would have been unemployed and the Japanese would have been employed producing our goods. The minister knows that is the , case. The minister knows that Japan invaded the British markets until she undersold British manufacturers right in Britain. She did the same thing in India.
That occurred in 1934 and 1933, and the only possible means of resisting it was the embargo and the quota method. How would you propose to deal with a situation like that? What Japan did was this. She had a population who were able to live on a ration of rice, so that she could produce ever so much more cheaply than the rest of us. We could not reduce our people in North America to the level of a rice diet. That is plain common sense. Not only that, but Japan discovered a means of subsidizing exports; she used her national credit for that purpose, so that her exporters could undersell all the rest of us. The result was that she beat us in every market of the world, and the fact that we adopted the system of quotas and embargos, which stopped her, was what seems to have driven her to war.
What would you do with a situation like that under the Bretton Woods agreement if you did not use quotas and embargos in the United States and in the Dominion of Canada? That is what I am trying to get at. The minister, I think, sees that is impossible. He said that he did not propose to interfere with freedom of trade.
