But that is ordinary government financing; it is what we call debt financing, as I understand that expression. What is Bretton Woods to a very humble person like myself who is not en famille, or 'en raport or en something or another with all these fancy fellows who write books and pamphlets? I have the largest waste-paper basket in the House of Commons. I do the best I can to read these things, which are gratuitously sent me

I do not pay for any of them-and yet that basket seems to grow day by day. The strong man who empties it must be a man indeed.
Here is my only thought of Bretton Woods, from my humble point of view. It is far from perfect. It has not these sanctions and so on. It does not compel one country to deliver such and such goods. What is it? It is a meeting of the minds of many nations. You do not get the end result there; but you perhaps get a start, and to me that is all that Bretton Woods is. It is a start in the control of exchange or currencies, so that, that start having been made, other trade agreements, multilateral I hope, may flow from it. I wish it had gone farther. I am sure there is no one in this House of Commons who does not so wish. But when you get all these people together you do not expect the maximum; you may get the minimum, but you expect the greatest amount of agreement that can be attained. I am for Bretton Woods for that reason. I have either listened to or read everything that has been said, and I have not yet heard one definite alternative to Bretton Woods.
It is all right to talk theories. We are told we should get all nations together and have an agreement of this or that kind. We had them together and this is the agreement we got. I am not for a moment discussing certain theories, and I probably could go a great deal farther with them than some hon. gentlemen to my left believe. They will at least admit that in the province of Alberta, in which I have lived all this time, I never

made one public utterance against social credit until the election that took place on June 11. At least I can say that in friendliness to those people down there.

Anyone who suggests that we can go back to the old conditions which prevailed after the last war has, in my judgment, not learned anything in the last twenty-five years. I am one of those people who believe that economically we are in a new era, and I am sure my hon. friends will agree with me in that. We cannot go back and make trade agreements with A, leaving out B, and making other agreements with C and D but not with G and probably Q; we cannot do that without destroying not only our own economy, because we would be the last to go, but the economy of the whole world.	-
Therefore I am with the minister in this. It is not a cure-all, and no one ever suggested it was. But I am with the Minister of Finance in saying that if we in this House of Commons do not go with the other nations as far as they have gone-and remember, Bretton Woods was not developed undter the new British government-then what are we doing? We are putting a spoke in the wheel of progress. This country and the world cannot wait. We must progress. Even those who drafted the agreements recognized that Bretton Woods is dangerous unless these other four recommendations can be implemented, but they make no suggestion as to how these recommendations can be implemented, and the minister has not a suggestion, not a single idea. All he can tell us is that there are arrangements for tariff reductions, but he cannot give a detailed answer to questions in connection with any of these matters. He cannot show that Belgium, for example, to protect its economy will not have to use every one of these trade restrictions to keep out cheap goods from the United' States. He cannot say that Great Britain will not have to adopt all these devices to keep the United States from literally flooding the British markets, putting the British people out of employment, and gaining such a control of British money that they can buy up British fixed assets to such an extent that they can own Britain outright. Now may I say to the hon. member for Calgary West-and I did admire the speech he made-it is true that we have gone into a new age; and the new age we have gone into is an age of abundance. It was foreshadowed in the speech from the throne; a resolution was placed on the order paper at an early stage in the session, and the reason it was not reached until now is that other legislative matters, which appeared to be of at least equal importance, were taken up.

I wish to point out, now that we are censured for not bringing this on until now, that we brought it on before it was brought on in the United Kingdom. I wish to point out also that in the United Kingdom it is not felt by the opponents of the Bretton Woods proposal that they must take week after week in an endeavour to defeat it. If we are to cause parliamentary institutions to command the respect of the people we must restrain ourselves a little bit in these discussions. The house gave an expression of its view on the, first reading of the resolution. The house was divided on it and the division was n.0 uncertain one. As I look at the record, the vote was 124 to 12 in favour of the resolution. In the light of that expression by the house, I would submit that my hon. friends ought to realize that the House of Commons as a whole is anxious that progress should be made, and made with this particular measure. There can be no objection at all to my hon. friends registering their opposition as strongly as they may wish to register it, but there is nothing to be gained by repeating and repeating and repeating; much less is there anything to be gained by unnecessarily straying to some extent beyond the motion which is before the committee for discussion and following also a course of procedure which causes many points of order to be raised.
I think it is essential and important in the business of parliament and in the interests of every hon. member of the house that at this time I should make plain that while the government is anxious to get through its business by the date I have mentioned, we are quite determined that what I have stated would be the remaining legislation for the session must be carried through before we prorogue. If we cannot conclude our work this week we shall have to go on before proroguing, and the government will have to consider whether we shall continue next week, or adjourn until after the Christmas recess, or until after the New Year. But we do intend to proceed with the rest of the measures I have said would be gone on with. That was understood and must be adhered to. In saying this, I am not saying anything that has not been already stated. It is not some new device to hasten the progress of any particular measure. It is simply to put the position clearly to the house.
What I should like to say to my hon. friends of the Social Credit group is this. The house knows now that they feel very strongly about the enactment of this measure. They have shown that, by opposing the resolution on the first reading, and they are showing it by debating it at considerable

length on the second reading. They have made their position very clear. But as the leader of the C.C.F. party has said, the bill itself has not yet been introduced, and my hon. friends know, particularly the hon. member for Lethbridge, that the right place at which to receive full information and details in regard to any bill, if it is going to a committee of the house, is before that committee, when the minister can have present the experts he may wish to have present, and where information can be given in detail. But it is not customary in the procedure of the house to take up the time of the house by seeking to get details on the resolution which precedes a bill, when it is understood that the bill itself is to go to a committee.
May I say one word further as to procedure when the bill comes before the committee. The government is placing no restriction on what may be done before the committee. Hon. members may seek all the information they desire and propose any amendments, and ,then when the bill comes back to the house from the committee it will go before the committee of the whole of this house. The government is placing no restrictions at all on what is to be discussed in the committee except the restrictions that the rules impose. There will be opportunities there for hon. gentlemen to express further their views and if they so ' desire to propose amendments. Again there is an opportunity for debate on the third reading of the bill, at which time, if hon. members feel necessarily so disposed, they can move amendments and vote against the measure.
With all that opportunity before them and realizing what the position is at this particular stage and what they know to be the wishes of hon. members generally, I ask my hon. friends of the Social Credit group if they could not be content, so far as this resolution is concerned, to register their position at this stage once and for all, and, having done so fully, allow the resolution to pass, the bill itself to be introduced and as it is now understood it will be, sent, after second reading, to the banking and commerce committee. Unless they adopt that course I am afraid that their position will be understood by this house to be one of obstruction and will be so viewed by the country.
Up to the present time it has not been necessary for this government to take advantage of some of the rules which are intended to prevent obstruction.
I noticed in listening to the remarks of my hon. friend the member for Vancouver East, who is an old parliamentarian, that he said there were rules to stop unnecessary discussion. I hope I shall never have to suggest to the

house that we take advantage of certain rules to shorten unnecessary debate. That is the last thing the government would wish to do. But if debate does reach the point where it ceases to be debate and becomes by endless and unnecessary repetition and irrelevancies obstruction, the rules are there to protect the house and may have to be applied.
I again say to my hon. friends that I hope they will cooperate with all the other members of this house in enabling us to make progress at this stage. We can take only one stage at a time.

I should like to say just one
word with respect to the understanding that was had among the leaders of the groups who met with the Prime Minister. I think the group around me have respected that understanding. In fact I believe, sir, if you look over Hansard, you will find that we have built up a pretty substantial bank account on which to draw in respect of this measure. We have tried to observe that understanding and we did, I am sure, with respect to all the measures that preceded this one. But, I recall that at the time the further business of the house was discussed I asked that this measure be held over. I also suggested that it would probably touch off a pretty heavy discussion. I believe both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance will recall my mentioning that.
My recollection of a study of parliamentary procedure tells me that we have been drifting farther and farther away from what used to be one of its ancient and honourable practices, that of having the fullest possible discussion in just such a committee as this. Here is where the finest discussion can take place, and here is where the ministers who are under fire, as it were, are supposed to answer the questions that are put to them by the members. Otherwise how in the name of common sense can anybody ever determine whether or not the principle of a measure which is to be introduced is worthy of being introduced? That is exactly what we are trying to, establish. It is not obstruction. All the information we have tried to obtain is relevant to the whole problem. I believe I did make this statement a few minutes ago, and I wish to go this far in impressing it on the committee, that three important things have to be resolved before Bretton Woods can hope to have even an even chance of success.
The first is this: can the United Kingdom, for which we are very much concerned, pay its way with or without being relieved of the nightmare of its huge war debts?

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL
speechtext: What about Canada?

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL
speechtext:
Well, Canada is in the same
position in a way.
The second thing which has to be resolved is this:	can the United States find ways of
increasing the stream of spending within its domestic economy sufficiently fast to employ its new-found producing power, indisputable evidence of which I presented in this chamber last Friday night and Saturday?
The third question is: can the the United States create an import surplus large enough to prevent a chronic shortage of dollars?
I suggested that these questions ought to be weighed extremely carefully, because the penalties of the failure of Bretton Woods will be extremely heavy penalties for succeeding generations. It is in that spirit that we are attempting to establish here a basis of judgment; so that when the measure is brought before the banking and commerce committee we can have something to gO' on, some information which the minister is in a position to supply, in order that we can elicit from the witnesses there information which will enable us to make up our minds.
I would say this on behalf of my group: I will attempt to facilitate the business of this house to the utmost of my capability; but since I have around me men of undoubted integrity and deep convictions I cannot bludgeon them, and I do not intend to try to bludgeon them in this matter. They have the right to speak; it is their undoubted right in a committee of this kind to speak and get the information which is necessary for them to make up their minds and to know definitely what the situation is. I will do, my best to facilitate action; I just ask the committee to give us a bit more time to round up the case, and we will see what we can do about getting this out of committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for his promise of cooperation. My purpose in rising is to touch a little further on a- point of procedure which he himself has raised and which is the main point I am raising at the present time.
My hon. friend has said that this house is drifting, that we are getting away from ancient and honourable tradition. May I point out that this may be true, but if it is true it is the fault of his group, for this reason, that the ancient and honourable tradition of this house is not to debate a measure of this kind on the resolution; it is to debate it on the second reading of the bill or when the house is in, committee on the bill or on the third reading of the bill. It is not the tradition in this house, nor has it been the tradition in the British House of Commons to debate a measure at length upon the mov-
Bretton Woods Agreements

ing of the resolution which precedes its introduction. My memory goes back a certain distance in this house, and I can remember quite well that Sir Wilfrid Laurier-as far back as that, and there were also others before him-took very strong exception to the house spending its time in debating a resolution before the introduction of a bill. The' custom has changed to some extent, but I just want to say that I hope we shall not drift farther in that direction, especially when we have four parties in this house; otherwise we shall never get through its business. What I am pleading for is the fullest opportunity of every party to make its position perfectly plain, but that we follow if we can the custom of the British house, which is based on ancient and honourable tradition, and do what they do there: fix as largely as possible, a limit of definite time within which a debate is to take place. In a most important debate such as has been mentioned by the Minister of Finance to-night this very subject of Bretton Woods, combined with the great question of financial relations between the United * States and Britain, only two or three days has been set apart. It is the only way business can be carried through. We have taken nearly three days, as I understand it, on the resolution, and we have still to send the bill to the banking and commerce committee and to deal with it when it comes back from the committee. I do not wish to cause any hon. member to hesitate to speak; I do not think it will be thought I am attempting to bludgeon anyone; I am seeking to persuade hon. members to follow a course prescribed by the rules, which is in their interest as much as it is in the interest of all hon. members of the house to have strictly followed.	*

Until this session, as hon. members know, I have been leader of the Social Credit group in this house. Now I am going to ask if the Prime Minister or anyone in this house can accuse me of having been non-cooperative here with the government in its efforts to get through the business.
I think no one will raise a word against the record which our party has in this house. Indeed, we have been so cooperative that one man, whom I would name were it not for the fact that he has passed beyond the veil, went out into the election campaign in Alberta and told the people of that province that we were a weak and ineffective lot who did not really make our opinions felt. That alone ought to be sufficient answer to the Prime Minister, and it ought to be sufficient justification in this,, house for the amount of attention we are giving this measure.

It just happens that, because of the peculiar nature of the social credit movement, it has become necessary for that movement to understand finance and trade. The result is that this particular measure is one upon which we are more or less specialists.

My hon.
friend has made a reference to myself, and before he proceeds I should like to supplement that I have said by quoting from Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, page 168, section 439:
The object of the resolution recommended by the crown is to give the house a first opportunity to discuss the advisability of making a certain expenditure. The details of the projected measure are not then disclosed and debate is confined to the resolution, which should not be lengthy, although care must be taken that the terms used are sufficiently wide to cover the whole of the bill which will be subsequently introduced.
It is perfectly clear that the rules of the house are that a resolution is simply to give members an opportunity to discuss the advisability of making certain expenditures, reserving for other stages fuller discussion. That is all I ask my hon. friends to do.

I must be impressed by any reading of the rules of the house; yet I wish to read another rule. Before I do so, however, I would call the Prime Minister's attention to the fact that the item under discussion at. the present time is not money that is to be spent-not by any means. If it were an offer to spend five billions I would not object. It is not the spending of money; it is the risk of liberty-that is the point-and the risk of war. We are not discussing a money problem at all. If we were, the rule which the Prime Minister has read would apply. But since we are discussing what we are, may I read to the house standing order 58:	[DOT]
The standing orders of the house shall be observed in the committees of the whole house so far as may be applicable, except the standing orders as to the seconding of motions and limiting the number of times of speaking.
If that rule does not indicate quite clearly that the committee of the whole, on a resolution, is for the purpose of allowing members to ask every kind of question they deem advisable, in order to get information of every kind which they desire to obtain from a minister, then I should like to know why the rule is there. I think that is an answer to the Prime Minister.
Let me now turn to the speech which was made by the minister when discussing Bretton Woods. I would quote from page 3040 of Hansard, and I will ask the minister for explanations of certain terms which he uses.
I presume that the speech which the minister gave in the house was designed to convince the house of the expediency of the measure. It is important to know what he meant by the terms he used when he said:
This conference was held after a couple of years of intensive discussion among the treasury officials of a large number of united nations.
May I ask the minister who originated the Bretton Woods agreement. Was it originated in Canada, and, if so, by whom? In the United States, and, if so, by whom? Or in Great Britain, and, if so, by whom, and at whose instigation, so far as is known?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL
speechtext: It originated as set out in the papers that were tabled in this house, the document entitled, "International stabilization of currencies", which was printed and tabled in this house, I believe in 1943. There were two or three papers prepared. The document contains the text of a paper setting out proposals by British experts for an international clearing union, and the text of the statement on international stabilization of currencies presented to the United States senate committee on April 5, 1943, as well as the text and draft outline of a proposal by United States experts for united and associated nations stabilization fund. Then the Canadian experts produced, about that time or shortly afterwards, a document entitled "Tentative draft proposals of Canadian experts for an international exchange union".

Convertibility of foreign-held balances.
(a) Each member shall buy balances of its currency held by another member if the latter, in requesting the purchase, represents
(i)	that the balances to be bought have been recently acquired as a result of current transactions; or

The question I should like to ask the minister is this. If a member does not possess gold, how can it buy its currency with gold? It merely states that a member shall buy its currency in gold. Who is to provide , that nation with gold if it is not a gold producer? That is all very well for nations like Canada, the United States, Russia and South Africa and the nations that are heavy gold producers, but what about those nations which are not gold producers?
